Disease Outbreak Disrupts Tunisia’s Engineering & Construction Projects

A sudden outbreak of Legionnaires’ disease among construction workers has disrupted engineering and construction activities across several major sites in northern Tunisia, industry officials and union representatives confirmed on Wednesday. The outbreak, first detected late last week near Bizerte, has resulted in the hospitalization of at least 47 workers and prompted temporary suspension of operations at multiple large infrastructure projects.

The National Federation for Engineering and Construction (FNEC) reported that five ongoing public works sites, including highway expansions and municipal water system upgrades, have been partially or fully shut down as health authorities investigate the source of the infection. “The safety of our workforce is paramount, and we are cooperating closely with the Ministry of Health,” said FNEC spokesperson Mourad Ben Youssef. “At this stage, work stoppages are unavoidable as we assess and sanitize affected areas.”

Legionnaires’ disease, a severe form of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, is typically contracted by inhaling contaminated water droplets. Preliminary investigations by the Tunisian Office of Occupational Health point to a malfunctioning cooling system at a major site in Menzel Bourguiba as the probable origin. “We are conducting environmental testing at all sites where cases have been reported,” said Dr. Hanen Jerbi, who is leading the official inquiry. “Our priority is to prevent further transmission and ensure workers receive appropriate medical care.”

The immediate impact on project timelines is already apparent. According to industry estimates, work delays range from one week to more than a month, depending on the scale of the site and the number of infected workers. “Some projects were already behind schedule due to supply chain challenges earlier this year,” noted Amine Trabelsi, an independent construction sector analyst in Tunis. “This outbreak compounds existing difficulties and may push completion dates well into 2025.”

Union representatives have called for enhanced safety protocols and urgent government support. “Many workers are concerned not only about their health but also about lost wages,” said Latifa Gharbi, regional secretary of the Construction Workers’ Union. She urged contractors to provide paid leave for affected staff and to accelerate installation of new safety measures, including regular water system inspections and on-site medical checks.

The Ministry of Health confirmed that mobile clinics have been dispatched to affected construction zones and that contact tracing is underway. “We are working around the clock to contain the outbreak and support workers,” said a ministry official.

As of Wednesday afternoon, officials could not provide a definitive timeline for the resumption of normal operations across all sites. The FNEC warned that further disruptions are possible as the investigation continues.
